title: end-to-end-variance-http2-grpc-chunking-experiments-may-2026
content:
Summary:

Hands-on experiment log exploring client-observed variance for streaming responses over HTTP/2 and gRPC under different chunking strategies, proxy configurations (Envoy vs nginx), and simulated slow clients. Goal: explain sporadic p95/p99 spikes that customers see even when median latency is fine, and surface mitigations.

High-level findings (TL;DR):
- Small, frequent chunks (<= 256B) cause high p99 amplification when proxies perform per-chunk buffering or when TLS record coalescing occurs; median unaffected but p95/p99 increase 1.5–3x relative to larger chunks.
- gRPC (HTTP/2) with default flow-control windows is more resilient to client slowness than raw HTTP/1.1 chunked, but only when connection multiplexing is healthy (no head-of-line at proxy).
- Envoy with default buffer limits introduced 20–80ms tail latency per chunk at high QPS in our env; tuning upstream/downstream buffer limits and HTTP/2 frame limits reduced p99 by ~30ms.
- Keep-alive and connection reuse matter: per-request TLS handshake adds ~70–120ms tail depending on region; reuse cut tail latency dramatically.
- Observed interactions between Nagle/TCP_NODELAY and small writes from server runtime: disabling Nagle for streaming sockets reduced token-to-token jitter for very small chunk sizes in local tests.

Experiment setup:
- Serving runtime image: rwinf/serving-runtime:canary-2026-05 (same binary used in production smoke).
- Models: small autoregressive toy model (latency ~5ms/token) and medium Llama-8B optimized (latency ~18ms/token) to test both CPU and GPU token pacing.
- Clients: synthetic generator that can simulate ideal client (always reading) and slow client (delays reading 0–250ms randomly per chunk).
- Proxies: Envoy (v1.26) and nginx (1.25) configured as streaming front proxy.
- Network: within us-west cluster (low baseline jitter) and a simulated inter-region path (adds 25ms base RTT and 1% packet loss).
- Measured metrics: end-to-end token latency distribution per request (first-token, inter-token, final-token), connection setup cost, CPU/IO wait on server, proxy queue durations.

Test matrix (representative):
- Chunk sizes: 128B, 512B, 2KB, 8KB
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 (gRPC streaming), HTTP/2 with application-level framing (single large message every N tokens)
- Client behavior: fast, moderate (30ms read delay), slow (random 10–200ms delay)
- Proxy: none (direct), Envoy default, Envoy tuned, nginx streaming config
- QPS levels: 50, 250, 1000 (to exercise proxy memory limits)

Representative numbers (p50/p95/p99 in ms, end-to-end for inter-token after steady-state generation):
- direct + gRPC + 8KB chunks + fast client @250QPS: p50=20ms p95=36ms p99=58ms
- envoy default + gRPC + 128B chunks + slow client @250QPS: p50=22ms p95=220ms p99=410ms
- envoy tuned + gRPC + 128B chunks + slow client @250QPS: p50=21ms p95=110ms p99=170ms
- nginx + HTTP/1.1 chunked + 512B chunks + moderate client @250QPS: p50=25ms p95=95ms p99=140ms
- direct + HTTP/1.1 + 2KB chunks + fast client @250QPS: p50=28ms p95=48ms p99=72ms

Notes on artifacts and causes:
1) Per-chunk stalls at proxies: Envoy's stream buffer limits cause backpressure: when downstream client stops reading, Envoy buffers incoming frames up to buffer_size, then starts applying backpressure to upstream (with internal queuing). When chunk sizes are tiny, the number of framing operations and the interplay with HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE pacing lead to queuing microbursts that surface as high tail latency.
2) TLS and TCP interactions: TLS record boundaries plus Nagle can delay small writes until enough payload accumulates. In practice, runtime was writing per-token (10–200B writes). Turning off Nagle (TCP_NODELAY) and doing write coalescing at runtime (batch tokens into 1–2KB writes) reduces jitter.
3) Client read slowness: slow clients holding the connection open result in proxies switching to buffering mode or reducing concurrency to that connection. This elevates p99 for other connections when proxy memory gets fragmented.
4) gRPC vs HTTP/1.1 differences: gRPC/HTTP2 benefits from multiplexing multiple streams over single connection but is more susceptible to head-of-line blocking if server sends large frames that saturate stream window or if proxy implementation serializes writes. HTTP/1.1 chunked can be simpler in proxying systems but loses the multiplexing gains.

Troubleshooting logs and traces (where to look):
- Server side: token emission timestamps (server runtime should log per-token send-ts and bytes), socket write syscalls (strace) when reproducing locally, and TLS record sizes (openssl s_server verbose).
- Envoy: admin /stats and /clusters for buffer events, and debug logs for HTTP/2 flow control. Look for upstream_rq_pending_active and http2.rx_reset_stream counters.
- Nginx: proxy_buffering and proxy_max_temp_file_size usage; error_log level debug to see proxy buffering behavior.
- Client: tcpdump and pcap to observe small TLS records or large coalesced records; instrumented client timestamps to measure read() delays.

Config tweaks that materially helped in experiments (prioritized):
1) Increase Envoy upstream and downstream buffer limits and tune http2.max_concurrent_streams + per-stream window sizes (reduced p99 by ~30ms in our tests).
2) Implement server-side token batching: instead of write per token, batch 2–8 tokens (configurable by latency budget) into each write. This reduced p99 by 20–120ms depending on chunk size and client slowness.
3) Set TCP_NODELAY on streaming sockets to avoid interaction with Nagle for very small writes when batching can't be applied.
4) Add intelligent proxy timeouts and circuit-breaker that prefer closing very slow connections earlier rather than allowing them to consume proxy buffer memory indefinitely.
5) Use keep-alive pools in clients to avoid frequent TLS handshakes for short-lived streams.

Potential mitigations we should evaluate next (actionable items):
- Adaptive chunking algorithm in runtime: dynamically increase batch size when observing downstream stall (client read lag) and reduce when downstream is reading fast. We sketched a local algorithm: monitor write() latency and ACK pacing, if per-write syscall latency > 20ms over 3 samples, increase batch size by 2x up to 8KB.
- Proxy-aware headers: advertise expected streaming chunk size in an initial header so proxies can pre-allocate buffers (requires Envoy/nginx config support).
- Per-customer QoS policy: map slow-client-suspect to lower memory allocations/buffers or move to dedicated worker pools.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much of this shows up for our hosted API customers vs internal Dedicated clusters with different proxy topologies? Need sampling from real traces (span annotations for per-token timing) to quantify.
- Interaction with HTTP/3 (QUIC): QUIC doesn't have head-of-line at transport layer the same way—might help. We should run a small set of HTTP/3 experiments with proxy that supports it.
- Resource cost of increasing Envoy buffers across fleet: memory vs tail latency trade-off. Estimate needed.

Action items (owners):
- Add per-token timestamps to production traces (Priya) — Linear RINF-3421 (see linked).
- Implement server-side batching knobs and TCP_NODELAY switch (Maya + Samir) — draft PR in repo (linked).
- Run controlled A/B on small set of customers: Envoy tuned vs default (Diego) — prepare canary plan.
- Investigate HTTP/3 feasibility and run 1-week micro-bench (Samir).

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing locally:
1) Launch runtime: docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 rwinf/serving-runtime:canary-2026-05 with TOKEN_BATCHING=1 (or 0 for baseline).
2) Start envoy with envoy.yaml (attached in repo) and default buffer limits; also start tuned envoy with buffer limits increased.
3) Run client generator: python tools/stream-client-gen.py --protocol grpc --chunk-size 128 --client-delay 0,200 --qps 250 --duration 600s
4) Collect p50/p95/p99 inter-token metrics and capture tcpdump for first 60s.

Notes-to-self: keep this doc as the canonical troubleshooting template for networking-induced tail latency in streaming. Will fold into Confluence after internal review.
